result.question: What is the publication landscape for protein variant effect prediction benchmark papers in 2024-2026? Specifically: (1) Which journals publish computational biology benchmarks like ProteinGym - Nature Methods, Genome Biology, Bioinformatics, NAR, PLOS Comp Bio, Briefings in Bioinformatics - what are their impact factors, acceptance rates, review times, and open-access policies? (2) Do these journals allow preprints on arXiv or bioRxiv before/during/after submission - what are their exact preprint policies? (3) Does putting code and data on GitHub before submission void peer review or count as prior publication? (4) What makes a benchmark paper in this space publishable - what do reviewers look for, how many models need to be evaluated, what's the minimum dataset size? (5) What are the fastest routes to publication for a novel benchmark - any journals with accelerated review for software/data papers? (6) Are there examples of benchmark papers that were GitHub-first then published (like ProteinGym itself)?
result.summary: The publication landscape for protein variant effect prediction benchmark papers in 2024-2026 spans both computational biology journals and major ML conferences. Top ML venues (NeurIPS Datasets & Benchmarks, ICML) have emerged as prestigious and viable routes, with ProteinGym (NeurIPS 2023) and FLIP2 (ICML 2026 Oral) as prominent examples. All major computational biology journals — Nature Methods, NAR, Bioinformatics, PLOS Comp Bio — explicitly permit preprints on bioRxiv/arXiv at any stage without treating them as prior publication, and none treat GitHub code/data deposits as prior publication; Bioinformatics actually requires code on GitHub at submission time. Benchmark scale in published work ranges from ~23 models (focused benchmarks) to 70+ (ProteinGym), with dataset sizes spanning hundreds of thousands to millions of variants across dozens of DMS assays, though no journal specifies hard numerical minimums. Fast-track review exists (Biology Open achieved 4.6 business day mean in a pilot), and Bioinformatics Application Notes offers a compact 4-page format for software/data tools.

findings.claim: Major ML conferences (NeurIPS, ICML) are established, prestigious venues for protein variant benchmark papers — not just computational biology journals.
findings.evidence: ProteinGym was published in NeurIPS 2023 Datasets and Benchmarks Track (official proceedings confirmed). FLIP2 was accepted at ICML 2026 as an Oral presentation (top ~0.7%), described as Spotlight top 2.2% on the project website. Both papers evaluate computational models for protein fitness/variant effect prediction, confirming ML conferences actively accept and recognize benchmark contributions in this space.

findings.claim: Nature Methods explicitly allows preprint posting on bioRxiv, arXiv, or author websites before, during, or after submission; this does not constitute prior publication and does not affect consideration or review. Preprint server manuscripts are also not factored into novelty assessment.
findings.evidence: Nature Methods editorial policy states: 'preprints may be posted at any time during the peer review process. Posting of preprints is not considered prior publication and will not jeopardize consideration at Nature Portfolio journals.' A separate policy clause states: 'Manuscripts posted on preprint servers will not be taken into account when determining the advance provided by a study.' Both policies confirmed via official Nature Portfolio editorial policy pages. The 2016 Nature Methods editorial (nmeth.3831) endorsed bioRxiv and arXiv specifically. Policy confirmed stable through 2025-2026.

findings.claim: NAR explicitly permits preprint deposits on arXiv and bioRxiv before or during submission, does not treat such deposits as prior publication, and does not treat GitHub code/data deposits as prior publication either. Authors must update preprint records upon acceptance.
findings.evidence: NAR policies page states verbatim: 'NAR allows authors to deposit preprints in community preprint servers such as arXiv.org and BioRxiv.org, provided that entries are updated to acknowledge that the article has been accepted/published by NAR.' A 2019 NAR editorial confirmed no restrictions on pre-submission posting and that such posting is not treated as prior publication. The same policy page recommends GitHub as a code repository without designating it as prior publication. The policy requires work be 'original, previously unpublished' but this refers to peer-reviewed venues. One nuance: the Methods criteria state methods already applied and published (even without full technical detail) may be ineligible — this concerns peer-reviewed results, not GitHub deposits.

findings.claim: Bioinformatics (Oxford) permits preprints on bioRxiv/arXiv at all stages without treating them as prior publication, and actively requires code to be publicly available on GitHub or equivalent stable URLs at the time of submission — meaning GitHub-first code release is not only permitted but mandated.
findings.evidence: Author guidelines state: 'As an author, you retain the right to make an Author's Original Version (preprint) available through various channels and this does not prevent submission to the Journal.' Separately, for software submissions: code must be 'freely available at stable URLs (e.g. github, bitbucket) without request to non-commercial users at the time of submission.' The journal also offers a bioRxiv direct-transfer integration. The logical implication is unambiguous: GitHub pre-release cannot void peer review when the journal mandates it as a condition of submission.

findings.claim: Bioinformatics offers a dedicated Application Notes article type (up to 4 pages) for novel software, algorithm implementations, and databases — requiring only that software or data be freely available to non-commercial users. This is a compact fast-route format for benchmark tools.
findings.evidence: Author guidelines confirm Application Notes covers 'novel software or new algorithm implementations, databases and network services,' limited to approximately 2,600 words or 2,000 words plus one figure (~4 pages), with the requirement that 'Software or data must be freely available to non-commercial users.' This format is suitable for benchmark tools and databases that do not require extensive biological narrative.

findings.claim: PLOS Computational Biology allows preprint deposition on bioRxiv and other servers before, during, and after submission without affecting manuscript consideration, and actively facilitates direct bioRxiv-to-journal transfers.
findings.evidence: Submission guidelines state verbatim: 'Deposition of manuscripts with preprint servers does not impact consideration of the manuscript at any PLOS journal.' The journal offers opt-in bioRxiv integration during initial submission. Minor carve-outs exist for preregistered research articles, which are ineligible for facilitated preprint posting, but this does not affect the general policy.

findings.claim: NAR Web Server Issue requires software to be fully functional and tested at submission, with comparison to existing methods and demonstrated novelty, but specifies no minimum number of benchmarked models or minimum dataset size. GigaByte Journal formally accepts preprint submissions and was founded on a preprint-promoting 'Publish, Review, Curate' model.
findings.evidence: NAR Web Server guidelines state: 'The software must be completely functional and have been extensively tested at the time of submission. Comparison to existing methods should be included.' No numerical minimum for benchmarked models or dataset size is specified anywhere in the guidelines. GigaByte's founding editorial (articles/1) contains the text 'Preprint submitted to: https://doi.org/10.31229/osf.io/hj7wx,' confirming the editorial itself was posted as a preprint, and the journal's FAQ confirms it cross-links to preprint versions in article metadata.

findings.claim: Published benchmark papers in this space evaluate roughly 20-70+ models. ProteinGym (NeurIPS 2023) covers ~2.7M missense variants across 217 DMS assays and ~300k indel mutants across 74 DMS assays. A focused benchmark (VenusMutHub, 2025) evaluated 23 models across sequence-only, evolution-informed, and structure-aware categories — suggesting 20+ models is a credible lower bound for publication, though larger benchmarks set a higher standard.
findings.evidence: ProteinGym (NeurIPS 2023) benchmarks 217 substitution DMS assays (~2.7M missense variants) and 74 indel DMS assays (~300k mutants), evaluating 40+ models at publication (leaderboard has since grown to 70+). VenusMutHub (PMC12144947, Acta Pharmaceutica Sinica B) evaluated exactly 23 models across three categories. No journal sets hard numerical minimums. The field norm appears to be: the more comprehensive the model coverage, the higher the likely venue; but focused benchmarks with 20+ models remain publishable in reputable journals.

findings.claim: Fast-track peer review routes exist for computational biology papers. A pilot at Biology Open (Company of Biologists) achieved a mean review turnaround of 4.6 business days across 20 manuscripts, with 100% meeting the 7-business-day target.
findings.evidence: The bioRxiv preprint (10.1101/2025.03.18.644032) and its corresponding published Biology Open article both report: 100% of Fast & Fair peer review pilot manuscripts met the turnaround target, with a mean of 4.6 business days across 20 manuscripts. A 2026 follow-up preprint reports 5.5 working days at expanded scale. Caveat: this is a self-reported pilot by journal editors, n=20, and the journal (Biology Open) is not a top-tier venue for computational benchmarks. Its relevance is as evidence that fast-track mechanisms exist in principle in this publishing ecosystem.

result.caveats:
1. Policy currency: journal policies can change; all findings reflect confirmed policies as of 2025-2026 sources, but authors should verify current policies at submission time. The Nature Methods and NAR policies were confirmed via live page fetches in the adversarial verification phase.

2. Impact factors and acceptance rates: none of the 17 confirmed claims addressed these metrics directly, and the adversarial verification process did not produce surviving claims on journal impact factors or acceptance rates. These metrics were either not researched or did not survive verification — they are an open gap.

3. The 'GitHub-first then published' narrative for ProteinGym: two claims attempting to establish this were refuted (0-3 votes each), so the finding about ProteinGym's GitHub release strategy is absent from confirmed claims. This does not mean it is false — it means the verifiers could not confirm it from available sources.

4. Minimum dataset size and model count are genuinely unspecified by any journal. The numbers cited (23 models, ~2.7M variants) are descriptive of what has been published, not prescriptive thresholds. Reviewers likely assess comprehensiveness relative to the paper's scope.

5. Biology Open's fast-track pilot is self-reported, small (n=20), and from a journal not specialized in computational benchmarks. It demonstrates proof-of-concept for fast review, not a standard practice across the target venues.

6. FLIP2's acceptance was verified as Oral (top ~0.7%), which is higher than the Spotlight (top 2.2%) label on its project website — if anything the claim understates the recognition level.
openQuestions: What are the current impact factors and acceptance rates for Nature Methods, Genome Biology, Bioinformatics, NAR, PLOS Comp Bio, and Briefings in Bioinformatics specifically for computational biology benchmark papers? These were not covered by the surviving confirmed claims.

Do Genome Biology and Briefings in Bioinformatics have the same preprint-permissive policies as the other journals surveyed? Both were named in the original question but no surviving confirmed claims addressed their specific policies.

What specific reviewer criteria distinguish a publishable benchmark paper from one that is 'merely an engineering contribution' in the eyes of Nature Methods versus Bioinformatics — i.e., how much biological insight or novel scientific finding (beyond the benchmark itself) do top-tier venues require?

Is there a GitHub-first-then-published precedent specifically for ProteinGym or FLIP (the original), where the codebase and data were demonstrably public before peer review concluded? The adversarial verification refuted two claims attempting to establish this, leaving the question open.

refuted.claim: ProteinGym benchmarks over 40 models across multiple categories (single-sequence, MSA-based, structure-informed, and multimodal), setting a de facto minimum scale for competitive benchmark papers in this space.

ProteinGym was GitHub-first: the codebase, datasets, MSAs, structures, and model predictions were all open-sourced prior to or alongside publication, with versioned releases (v1.0 through v1.3) showing ongoing post-publication expansion — demonstrating that public GitHub/data release does not preclude NeurIPS publication.
PLOS Computational Biology publishes benchmarking papers as a recognized article type, provided they include comprehensive benchmarks with reproducible metrics.
Springer Nature explicitly states that pre-publication data sharing will not be considered prior publication, covering Nature journals and BMC journals.

This benchmark used 905 small-scale experimental datasets spanning 527 proteins, suggesting that a dataset of this scale (hundreds of proteins, nearly a thousand experimental datasets) is considered sufficient for a publishable benchmark in this space.

GigaByte Journal publishes Data Release and Technical Release articles focused on datasets and software/computational workflow papers, with no article processing charges for the first 6 months and subsequent APCs well under the European mean of approximately $2160.

NAR Web Server Issue papers have a strict length limit of 4-5 printed journal pages, not a standard research article format, making it unsuitable for comprehensive benchmark papers requiring extensive methodology and results sections.

FLIP2 code and data are publicly released on GitHub (https://github.com/J-SNACKKB/FLIP) and Zenodo under CC-BY 4.0 or MIT licenses, demonstrating that GitHub-first data/code release is compatible with subsequent peer-reviewed publication at a top venue.
